units: a damp upland place gathers several natural habitats into a small area
a waterlogged plant carpet borders the pool
organisms fixed to the stone withstand a lack of water
hollow stems serve as shelter for young insects
the water looks clear but carries scraps of plant matter
tiny near-transparent animals move in short bursts
seeds buried in the bottom wait for a favourable period
every level depends on the others and losing one leaves the whole poorer
text: A high mountain bog brings together several quite unlike habitats within a very small stretch of ground. Along the pool spreads a carpet of sodden moss; it gives way underfoot, then springs back at once. Higher up, bare rock wears a coat of grey lichen, rough to the touch, which survives one drought after another. Between the two grow tall grasses whose hollow stems shelter minute larvae. The water counts as a habitat of its own. It looks clear from above, yet it carries scraps of plant matter that cloud it the moment you stir it. See-through insects dart about in short bursts, all but invisible. Deeper down, under the silt, seeds lie dormant and wait for a kinder season before they sprout. Every one of these layers leans on the rest, and losing a single one leaves the whole poorer.

units: artificial lighting was aimed first at the safety of public roads
it then spread to buildings and to parking areas
commercial signs shine at night above empty walkways
only the brightest stars stay visible
an orange glow hides the depth of the sky
migrating birds circle the lit buildings
insects active after sunset die beside the lamps
some local authorities have already switched the lighting off in the middle of the night without complaint
text: We have mislaid the night sky, and hardly anyone noticed. It began sensibly enough: street lamps went up so that people could walk home without fear. Then the glare crept onto building fronts, onto car parks, onto shop windows, and we took it for granted. Now signs blaze away till dawn above empty pavements. Look up and you get a handful of the fiercest stars, nothing else, since an orange wash has swallowed whatever lies behind them. Birds on migration steer by those stars, so they circle the lit towers until they drop. Moths and beetles that come out after sunset batter themselves against the lamps and die at the foot of them. Switching off after midnight would cost us little. Several local authorities have done exactly that, and no resident grumbled. It seems a pity to wait until darkness is only a memory.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman leading the team explores a network of passages not yet mapped
a fall into a crack in childhood set off her calling
she found then a chamber crossed by falling water
her parents worked a dry sloping plot of land
she understood that the water missing at the surface travelled lower down
she trained in a field devoted to the study of waters
her measurements show the deep reserves refilling faster than expected
the neighbouring authorities changed where they draw water after these results
text: The scientist who leads the team spends her working weeks underground, in a run of passages that no survey had ever put on paper. Her calling began with a fall. As a child she slipped into a narrow crack in the family pasture and landed in front of a chamber with a sheet of water pouring through it. Her parents worked a dry patch of hillside, so she grasped early on that the water missing from the surface was travelling somewhere beneath it. She trained as a hydrologist, then came back to measure what she had glimpsed. Her readings show that the deep reserves refill far quicker than anyone assumed, and the authorities round about have since reworked where they draw their supply. The map she keeps updating now serves farmers and officials alike, and her quiet manner no longer stops people listening.

units: the exhibition deals with the marine depths
the first room shows animals kept in a liquid
this display conveys neither the pressure nor the darkness of the depths
the end of the route puts this fault right
a lightless passage forces the visitor to move forward blind
projected images show jelly-like animals above people's heads
a shudder of the floor goes with that scene
the writer regrets that this choice was not applied from the start
text: You leave this exhibition on the deep sea feeling you have brushed against something vast that has been poorly served. The weakness shows in the opening room, where cabinet after cabinet holds pale specimens suspended in spirit, with nothing to suggest the crushing weight or the blackness they came from. Under a hard light, a fish that once glowed is merely another jar. The closing stretch of the route puts matters right. The designers have cut a lightless corridor there, and you edge along it by touch while projections send drifting jellyfish across the ceiling, high above your head. The floor shudders faintly. At last the intended effect arrives: a crushing body of water, thinly peopled by rare creatures. Had that instinct governed the whole thing from the door onward, the most distracted visitor would have been won over.

units: the sender reports on two methods for tracking freshwater animals
the first method uses capture devices sunk into the water
the second consists of laying plates on the ground
the underside of the plates holds moisture
the sunken devices take more mature individuals
they call for regular visits and sometimes injure the animals' limbs
the plates give fewer captures but more reliable readings
a grainy material spread under the plates suits the young ones
the sender proposes splitting the two methods across two separate sectors
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I owe you of the two protocols we settled on for tracking the amphibians in the pond. One relies on smooth-walled traps sunk into the water. The other uses plates laid flat on the ground, the rough underside of which holds the damp. The traps take more adults, but somebody has to walk the line every second evening, and they often damage the animals' legs. Plates are put down once and draw only what is looking for shelter: the yield drops, though the data comes out cleaner. One more thing worth passing on. The gritty material we spread beneath the plates appears to suit the young ones while it hampers the adults. If you agree, let us keep the plates on the upper sector and the traps on the lower one, then set the catches side by side once the season closes.

units: a handful of forest soil holds a great many living things
the combined action of these things makes the ground fertile
threads that come from fungi extend the reach of the roots
these threads take up water and dissolved minerals
they receive in exchange sugary compounds made by the leaves
the tearing of this network lets the rain strip off the surface layer
restoring damaged ground takes several decades
the measures mentioned include covering with plant waste and keeping machinery off
dark springy crumbs show that the soil is recovering
text: What does a handful of forest soil hold? Fungal threads, bacteria, mites and worms, whose combined labour is the very thing that makes the ground fertile. And what do those threads do? They reach out well beyond the tree roots, take up water and dissolved salts, and trade them for sugars sent down from the leaves. What follows when that mesh is torn? The soil loses its grip, rain strips off the upper layer, and whatever grows back grows back poorer. Can ruined ground be repaired? It can, provided one accepts a timescale of several decades: the surface is covered with plant waste, machinery is kept off it, and deep-rooted species are put back to reopen the old channels. And what tells us it is working? Dark, springy crumbs that come apart between the fingers without turning to dust.

units: the forest warden advises coming before the female returns
the group sets off in the dark without a light
the assistant notes that the nest hole sits higher than the year before
the warden climbs with the help of a ladder
he draws a young bird covered in soft down out of the hole
the bird cannot stand yet
three other chicks occupy the cavity
the visitors measure the feathers and look at the colour of the bill
the female is back at the nest shortly after the group leaves
text: “Come up before the mother starts her rounds again, or you will see nothing,” the warden had told us the evening before. So we set off ahead of daylight with no torch, following the path by nothing more than the sound of our own feet. At the foot of the beech his assistant whispered that the hole sat higher than it had the year before. He hauled the ladder into position, slipped a hand inside the opening and drew out a chick still in soft down, not yet able to stand on its legs. “Three more behind it,” he said, and settled the bird back at the bottom of the nest. We took down the length of the feathers and the colour of the bill, and disturbed nothing else. “You watch, you count, you leave,” he added on the way down, summing up his trade. The mother was back at the nest soon after we had gone.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: quarry workers found the remains of shellfish in stone lying high up
these shapes were put down at first to a whim of the rock
stonecutters noticed that the remains were stacked in a steady order
this stacking recalled the floor of still water
the same order turned up in different valleys
the explanation by chance became hard to believe
observers put forward that the stone had formed under water
this idea implied that the ground had been pushed up
the notion was accepted because what it predicted held up in the field
text: Picture the faces of the quarrymen who split a slab high above the sea and found shells lying right across the stone. For generations the answer was that the rock had simply amused itself, that it could mimic living things when it chose. Then sharper-eyed stonecutters noticed the shells were stacked in beds, in an order that never varied, exactly as they settle on the floor of a quiet bay. Since that same order turned up in one valley after another, chance became an awkward thing to believe in. Some observers put forward an unwelcome answer: the rock had formed beneath the water, and the ground had later been pushed up. The idea took decades to gain a hearing, because it forced people to accept that hills move. It won in the end by predicting correctly. Where it promised marine beds, marine beds were found.

units: a watercourse penned between straight walls sheds its water too quickly
the water reaches the lower ground abruptly in heavy rain
the low parts of built-up areas go under
the bed dries out with the first spell of real heat
the straight channel had been dug to win farming ground
that channel did away with the bends which slowed the water and let it soak in
the repair consists of handing the watercourse back a share of its former room
the works include breaking open the built banks and replanting trees
the floods grow less violent and a flow survives in dry weather
text: A river running dead straight between two concrete walls sheds its water far faster than it ought to. Hydrologists say the same thing after every flood: the whole volume lands downstream in one go, the low-lying streets go under, the water leaves, and the bed is dry by the first spell of real heat. That straight channel was dug to win ground for crops, and it did away with the bends where the flow used to slow and soak in. The remedy tried lately is to hand the river back a share of the room it once had. Built-up banks are broken open, old side channels are dug out again, trees go in whose roots knit the edges together. The water winds once more, spreads into meadows made for flooding and feeds the water table. Floods lose their punch, and a trickle survives the hot months.

units: the walkers climb a steep face and come down by the other
the face they climb is dry and stony
only short grasses grow in the cracks of the rock
the walkers' water runs out quickly on the way up
the change of face happens within a few strides at the top
the other face is deep in thick vegetation
very cold water seeps from the wall
a group of farm animals rests in the shade on that side
the narrator concludes that a hill is made of faces exposed in different ways
text: We had settled on climbing the steep face and coming down the other, with no notion at all of how sharply the two would turn out to contradict each other. The way up was dry and stony: baking slabs, tufts of cropped grass wedged into cracks, and the rasp of insects for company. Nothing there held any water, and our bottles emptied before our eyes. The switch came within three strides. Over the ridge lay a shaggy slope, deep in ferns, where the air smelt of wet moss. Threads of water seeped from the wall, cold enough to numb the fingers. We passed a flock grazing in the shade while the slope behind us went on roasting. One hill, cut in two by a ridge, was keeping two climates and two sets of living things. Since that walk, a mountain has never looked to me like one solid mass.
